- When sentiment is negative in the recent history (especially last 3–5 days), reduce forecasted peaks and avoid over-optimistic spikes.
- If model shows a sharp upward spike followed by a forecasted decline, check for mean reversion — often true price drops after peaks are exaggerated.
- For 30-day forecasts, if the model’s first few days are significantly higher than true outcome, apply a downward bias correction (e.g., subtract 1–2% of the forecasted value).
- If sentiment history shows strong bullish momentum (many +1s), model tends to overestimate — apply a 1–3% downward adjustment to the peak forecast.
- If sentiment turns bearish mid-period (e.g., -1.00 after +1s), model often overshoots the drop — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% of the peak value.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if model’s later days are too low (e.g., <75) while true outcome is still above 75, consider a slight upward bias to avoid premature mean reversion.
- If model consistently forecasts higher than true outcome in the first 5–7 days, apply a “lag correction” — reduce first 5–7 forecast values by 1–3% to reflect delayed reaction to sentiment.
